claims.text: The dynamic mechanical behavior of high-entropy alloys is explained by an interaction between lattice distortion and dislocation glide.
The interaction between lattice distortion and dislocation glide enhances strength and ductility.
The interaction between lattice distortion and dislocation glide promotes uniform deformation.
The interaction between lattice distortion and dislocation glide suppresses localized shear banding.
The proposed behavior applies to high-entropy alloys in either an as-cast or annealed initial state.
Strain rate and temperature are proposed as controlled variables during dynamic mechanical testing.
The proposed test domain spans strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
The proposed test domain spans temperatures from room temperature to 800°C.
Lattice distortion and dislocation density are the structural mediators of the dynamic mechanical response.
High-entropy alloys will have increased yield strength relative to conventional alloys with similar composition but without high-entropy characteristics.
High-entropy alloys will have increased uniform elongation relative to conventional alloys with similar composition but without high-entropy characteristics.
The hypothesis is bounded to high-entropy alloys containing a mixture of FCC and BCC structures.
The hypothesis is bounded to compositions having a high entropy of mixing, exemplified by a value greater than 1.5R.
A controlled comparison can vary lattice distortion and dislocation density and measure their relationship to yield strength and uniform elongation using in-situ TEM, XRD, and molecular dynamics.
Reduced strength and ductility relative to conventional alloys would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of correlation between lattice distortion or dislocation density and dynamic mechanical behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
